# CHAPTER X

POLITICAL MORALITY (1862)

On Moran's promotion to Secretary, Mr. Seward inquired whether Minister Adams would like the place of Assistant Secretary for his son. It was the first—and last—office ever offered him. To both, the change seemed useless: any young man could make some sort of Assistant Secretary; only one, just then, could make an Assistant Son. His position was abnormal—Court attaché by British courtesy, private secretary in the Legation, in society a young man without any position at all. Yet the irregular position lent itself to a sort of irregular education that seemed the only sort he was ever to get.

The spring and summer of 1863 saw a great change in Secretary Seward's management of foreign affairs. He felt at last that his representatives abroad needed support, and sent over every important American on whom he could lay his hands. The most interesting was Thurlow Weed, who took charge of the press and got into his hands the threads of management quietly and smoothly. Weed was a complete American education in himself—mind naturally strong, temper never ruffled, manners of benevolent simplicity in the tradition of Benjamin Franklin. The trait that astounded cynicism was his apparent unselfishness. He thought not of himself but of the person he was talking with; he grasped power, but not office; he gave, but he did not receive.

Management was an instinct with Mr. Weed; he played men like cards, taking them at face value. Once, after some stories strong even for the Albany lobby, the private secretary made bold to ask him outright: "Then, Mr. Weed, do you think that no politician can be trusted?" Mr. Weed hesitated, then said in his mild manner: "I never advise a young man to begin by thinking so."

At the time the lesson translated itself in a moral sense; later Adams thought Weed looked on it as a question of how the game should be played. Principles had better be left aside; values were enough. Seward also sent William M. Evarts as law counsel, an economist of morals with whom Adams grew intimate. "The world can absorb only doses of truth," Evarts said; "too much would kill it." One sought education in order to adjust the dose.

The teachings were practical, and the private secretary's life turned on their value. England's power of absorbing truth was small. Palmerston, Russell, Bethell, and the society of the *Times* offered a study that sickened a young student with anxiety. He had begun—contrary to Mr. Weed's advice—by taking their bad faith for granted. To settle whether he was right became the main object of an education laboriously pursued at stupendous cost.

The recognition of belligerency, the management of the Declaration of Paris, the Trent Affair—all strengthened the belief that Lord Russell had assumed, from May, 1861, that the Confederacy was established, and was waiting only for the proper moment to interpose. With the insolence of youth, Henry Adams jumped to the conclusion that Earl Russell, like other statesmen, lied; and although the Minister thought differently, he had to act as though Russell were false. The most costly tutors in the world were provided for him at public expense.

The demonstration began in June, 1862, with the imminent escape of "No. 290." On July 24, Collier's legal opinion warned: "It appears difficult to make out a stronger case of infringement of the Foreign Enlistment Act, which, if not enforced on this occasion, is little better than a dead letter." Four days afterwards, Earl Russell let the ship escape.

If one could not trust a dozen of the most respected private characters in the world, composing the Queen's Ministry, one could trust no mortal man. Lord Russell felt the force of the inference and undertook to disprove it. At first he threw the blame on the law officers; the lawyers overruled him. Then he pleaded guilty to criminal negligence: "I assent entirely to the opinion of the Lord Chief Justice of England that the Alabama ought to have been detained during the four days I was waiting for the opinion of the law officers.... It was my fault as Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs." Of course it was his fault. The true issue lay not in the question of his fault, but of his intent. To a young man getting an education in politics, there could be no sense in history unless a constant course of faults implied a constant motive.

For his father the question was practical; Minister Adams held the convenient belief that Russell was true, and died still holding it. His son wanted to know whether he could, in politics, risk trusting any one. The most curious fact was that Russell believed in his own good faith, and Argyll believed in it also. Westbury alone never professed to be moral, and on that ground was easier to read.

After the Alabama's escape on July 28, 1862, came the Union disasters before Richmond and at the second Bull Run, and Lee's invasion of Maryland, news of which reached England September 14. Palmerston instantly wrote to Russell: "If this should happen, would it not be time for us to consider whether in such a state of things England and France might not address the contending parties and recommend an arrangement on the basis of separation?" In 1889 Spencer Walpole published the official life of Earl Russell, and told a part of the story which had never been known to the Minister and which astounded his son.

Forty years later, Gladstone's own confession revealed that the Cabinet's drift toward intervention had been even nearer success than Adams had supposed; the lesson stood, that in politics no professed friend in power could be trusted, and that the diplomatic victory of 1862 had been won against men who scarcely knew their own minds.
